subject: Cognitive Science
title: How We Locate Sound
description: Learn How We Locate Sound in one minute.

hook.text: A twig snaps behind you and you spin instantly. Your brain computed the sound's location in microseconds.

buildup.text: Sound reaches your two ears at slightly different times. A sound to the left hits the left ear first.

discovery.text: The interaural time difference is tiny—about 600 microseconds maximum. Yet your brain resolves it precisely.

twist.text: For high-pitched sounds, timing cues fail. The brain switches to intensity differences—the head casts a sound shadow.

climax.text: Owls are so precise at sound localization that they catch mice in total darkness using hearing alone.

punchline.text: Two ears and a few microseconds are all you need to find danger.

quiz.question: How does the brain locate low-pitched sounds?
options: By comparing arrival time at each ear

details.summary: The brain locates sounds using tiny differences in timing and loudness between your two ears. A sound arriving slightly earlier and louder at one ear is perceived as coming from that side. The brain also uses the shape of the outer ear to estimate whether sounds come from above or below.
details.whyItMatters: Sound localization evolved to detect threats and navigate environments. Understanding it explains why two speakers create stereo illusions and why headphones simulate 3D audio.
takeaways: Interaural time and level differences indicate left-right position
The outer ear's shape helps determine up-down sound location
The brain fuses binaural cues into a single spatial percept

faq.question: How small are the timing differences the brain detects?
faq.answer: The brain can detect interaural time differences as small as 10 microseconds, which corresponds to a sound source displaced just one to two degrees from center. This extraordinary precision allows accurate localization even for brief sounds and operates entirely below conscious awareness.

faq.question: Why is it hard to locate sounds directly ahead or behind?
faq.answer: Sounds from directly ahead or behind produce identical interaural timing and level differences. The brain relies on subtle reflections from the outer ear and small head movements to resolve this front-back ambiguity. This is why you sometimes turn your head to locate an uncertain sound source.
